scenes.heading: Measures of centre and spread
scenes.sub: One number for typical, one for how spread out
scenes.say: How good is a player, and how reliable are they? You need two numbers: a centre for the typical value, and a spread for how far apart the values are.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Class photo line-up, shortest to tallest
scenes.science: Middle person = median; middles of each half = quartiles
scenes.breaks: With an even number of people, the median is halfway between the two middle people.
scenes.say: Picture everyone lined up for the school photo, shortest to tallest. The person in the very middle is the median. Split the line there, and the middle person of each half gives you the quartiles. The gap between those two shows how much the middle half of the class varies.

scenes.heading: Centre and spread
points: Median = middle value of ordered data
scenes.say: The mean is the sum divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value once the data is in order. The mode is the most common value. For spread, the range is largest minus smallest, and the interquartile range, or I Q R, is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile.

scenes.heading: Points in 11 games
scenes.question: 4, 7, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 15, 15, 21. Find the median and IQR.
scenes.say: Eleven games, already in order. The median is the sixth value, twelve. Because there's an odd number, leave twelve out of both halves. The lower half has middle value seven, so Q one is seven. The upper half has middle value fifteen, so Q three is fifteen. The I Q R is fifteen minus seven, which is eight.
scenes.caption: 11 games in order. The median is the 6th value, 12. Leave 12 out of both halves. Lower half: Q1 = 7. Upper half: Q3 = 15. IQR = 15 − 7 = 8.

scenes.heading: Quartiles on a number line
notes: The IQR covers the middle half
scenes.say: Here it is on a number line. First the line, then the three dots: Q one at seven, the median at twelve and Q three at fifteen. The bracket underneath covers the middle half of the data. Its length, eight, is the interquartile range.
scenes.caption: First the line, then Q1 at 7, the median at 12 and Q3 at 15. The bracket covers the middle half of the data. Its length, 8, is the IQR.

scenes.heading: Mean from a frequency table
scenes.say: This graph shows how many siblings twenty-five students have. Multiply each number of siblings by its frequency and add: thirty-six siblings in total. Divide by the twenty-five students, not the five columns. The mean is one point four four.
scenes.caption: Siblings of 25 students. Multiply each number of siblings by its frequency and add: 36 in total. Divide by 25 students, not 5 columns. Mean = 1.44.

scenes.heading: Which measures should you use?
scenes.say: If the data is roughly symmetric with no outliers, use the mean. If there's an outlier or a skew, use the median and the I Q R, because they barely move when one extreme value changes.

points: Frequency table: divide by total frequency
scenes.say: Quick recap. Always order the data first. Quartiles are the middles of the halves, and the I Q R is Q three minus Q one. In a frequency table, divide by the total frequency. With outliers, use the median and I Q R. Now try the practice questions!
